meta.description: Robin Williams didn't originate it. The earliest documented use (1982) credits comedian Charles Fleischer; Williams is one of many later misattributions.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you remember the '60s, you really weren't there'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Robin Williams. The line's earliest documented appearance (LA Times, 1982) credits comedian Charles Fleischer.

answer.label: Not Robin Williams — earliest credit goes to Charles Fleischer
answer.authorDates: b. 1950 · American comedian & actor (voice of Roger Rabbit)
answer.sourceLine: According to Quote Investigator, the earliest documented instance of this quip appeared in the Los Angeles Times “Comedy Column” of 13 June 1982, where it was used as an exit line by comedian Charles Fleischer. The line has since been pinned on Robin Williams, Paul Kantner, Timothy Leary, Grace Slick and others — but none of those attributions predates Fleischer’s, and QI awards him the credit until an earlier source surfaces.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from
source.excerpt: If you remember the ’60s, you really weren’t there.
trail: Quote Investigator locates the earliest instance in the Los Angeles Times “Comedy Column” of 13 June 1982, where comedian Charles Fleischer delivers it as an exit line.

QI notes the line has been attributed to Paul Kantner, Robin Williams, Paul Krassner, Pete Townshend, Grace Slick and Timothy Leary — and concludes that, until an earlier citation appears, Fleischer gets the credit.
Etymologist Barry Popik independently traces the same 1982 Fleischer citation and records the Robin Williams credit only appearing later, e.g. a 1989 newspaper attribution.
source.excerptNote: The joke is a paraprosdokian: the counterculture’s drugs and excess supposedly left true participants with no memory of the decade — so anyone who can recall it wasn’t really immersed in it.
source.rightsHolder: Los Angeles Times (1982 column); the quip as spoken by Charles Fleischer
source.rightsNote: The earliest documented appearance is a 1982 Los Angeles Times column, which is in-copyright. As a bare one-line joke the phrase itself is likely too short to attract independent copyright protection, but there is no pre-1931 or public-domain source to point to, so we do not treat it as public domain.

author.metaLine: b. 1950 · American stand-up comedian, actor & voice of Roger Rabbit
author.bio: Charles Fleischer (born 27 August 1950, Washington, D.C.) is an American stand-up comedian, actor and musician, best known as the voice of the title character in Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988). Long before that role, his stand-up one-liners circulated in newspaper comedy columns — including the 1982 exit line that is the earliest documented form of this quip.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a classic “magnet-name” quote: a clever one-liner that gets re-pinned on whichever counterculture-adjacent celebrity a poster finds most quotable — most often Robin Williams. None of those credits predates the 1982 newspaper citation.

items.why: Endlessly quote-carded to Williams (e.g. AZQuotes, Quotefancy), but Quote Investigator finds no evidence he originated it and lists him only as a later claimed source.

items.who: Paul Kantner, Timothy Leary, Grace Slick, Pete Townshend, Paul Krassner
items.why: All named as originators in various retellings, yet QI finds none with a citation earlier than Fleischer’s 1982 appearance.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented use is comedian Charles Fleischer’s exit line in the Los Angeles Times “Comedy Column” of 13 June 1982, per Quote Investigator — not Robin Williams.

context.heading: Why nobody can pin it down
lead: The joke is self-referential: it claims that anyone with clear memories of the 1960s must have missed the real, mind-altering experience of the decade. That built-in deniability is part of why it spread as folk wisdom with no fixed author — and why it attaches so easily to famous psychedelic-era names.

By the time Quote Investigator and etymologist Barry Popik went looking, the earliest hard citation they could find was a 1982 Los Angeles Times comedy column quoting Charles Fleischer. Everyone more famous who ‘said’ it — Williams, Leary, Kantner — shows up only later.
